   Before the split, the library used a single `:storage-state` key with a
   fragile heuristic (`contains '/'` → path, else JSON). The heuristic
   mis-classified inline JSON strings like `{"cookies":[{"path":"/"}]}`
   as paths — which caused HAR recording to silently break because the
   `.storageState()` roundtrip embeds `/` characters in every cookie. The fix:
   use an explicit key for each mode, no heuristic at all.

5df79bbbc874af49f4b28ee4d14047dc.name:
`stop-daemon!` ends in System/exit, which runs the JVM shutdown hook, which
   called `stop-daemon!` again — and System/exit inside a hook blocks forever
   while the exiting thread joins that hook. The resulting three-way deadlock
   (main ↔ hook ↔ idle timer) left a zombie daemon still holding its browser,
   with its socket and PID files already deleted, so every later command hit a
   dead socket and looked like 'the daemon is dying'.

59b3b79bd964583890fb1e081aa1d203.name:
A real daemon subprocess must be GONE after `close`.

   Regression test for the zombie daemon. `stop-daemon!` ended in System/exit,
   System/exit ran the JVM shutdown hook, and the hook called `stop-daemon!`
   again — System/exit from inside a hook blocks forever while the exiting
   thread joins that hook. The daemon logged `daemon stopping`, deleted its
   socket and PID file, answered the client, and then lived on forever holding
   its browser; even two SIGTERMs could not kill it. Every later command found
   a dead socket, so the CLI silently started ANOTHER daemon and the page,
   cookies and refs the script was using vanished.

   Asserting the close RESPONSE is what let this ship: the response was always
   correct. Only the process table proves the daemon is gone.

   fragile heuristic (`contains '/'` → path, else JSON). The heuristic
   mis-classified inline JSON strings like `{"cookies":[{"path":"/"}]}`

`stop-daemon!` ends in System/exit, which runs the JVM shutdown hook, which
   called `stop-daemon!` again — and System/exit inside a hook blocks forever
   while the exiting thread joins that hook. The resulting three-way deadlock
   (main ↔ hook ↔ idle timer) left a zombie daemon still holding its browser,
   with its socket and PID files already deleted, so every later command hit a
   dead socket and looked like 'the daemon is dying'. > human-duration — the span a user reads in the reason line > renders minutes, seconds and milliseconds

Regression tests for the `:storage-state` / `:storage-state-path` split.

   Before the split, the library used a single `:storage-state` key with a
   fragile heuristic (`contains '/'` → path, else JSON). The heuristic
   mis-classified inline JSON strings like `{"cookies":[{"path":"/"}]}`
   as paths — which caused HAR recording to silently break because the
   `.storageState()` roundtrip embeds `/` characters in every cookie. The fix:
   use an explicit key for each mode, no heuristic at all. > both keys together > allows both keys simultaneously (Playwright keeps whichever was set last internally)

d2f14f3c673afc0d14fc12aa404713b7.name:
A real daemon subprocess must be GONE after `close`.

   Regression test for the zombie daemon. `stop-daemon!` ended in System/exit,
   System/exit ran the JVM shutdown hook, and the hook called `stop-daemon!`
   again — System/exit from inside a hook blocks forever while the exiting
   thread joins that hook. The daemon logged `daemon stopping`, deleted its
   socket and PID file, answered the client, and then lived on forever holding
   its browser; even two SIGTERMs could not kill it. Every later command found
   a dead socket, so the CLI silently started ANOTHER daemon and the page,
   cookies and refs the script was using vanished.

   Asserting the close RESPONSE is what let this ship: the response was always
   correct. Only the process table proves the daemon is gone. > close makes the process exit and leaves no socket or PID behind

fb4a814f05da101d1374ff2d289af341.name:
`stop-daemon!` ends in System/exit, which runs the JVM shutdown hook, which
   called `stop-daemon!` again — and System/exit inside a hook blocks forever
   while the exiting thread joins that hook. The resulting three-way deadlock
   (main ↔ hook ↔ idle timer) left a zombie daemon still holding its browser,
   with its socket and PID files already deleted, so every later command hit a
   dead socket and looked like 'the daemon is dying'. > re-entrant stop > is a no-op while a stop is already in flight

Regression tests for the `:storage-state` / `:storage-state-path` split.

   Before the split, the library used a single `:storage-state` key with a
   fragile heuristic (`contains '/'` → path, else JSON). The heuristic
   mis-classified inline JSON strings like `{"cookies":[{"path":"/"}]}`
   as paths — which caused HAR recording to silently break because the
   `.storageState()` roundtrip embeds `/` characters in every cookie. The fix:
   use an explicit key for each mode, no heuristic at all. > :storage-state → setStorageState (inline JSON) > handles JSON containing cookie paths (the bug that motivated this split)
